concepts.name: Classification of Droughts: Four Types and Their Triggers
key_dimensions: Distinction between Meteorological, Hydrological, Agricultural, and Socioeconomic drought — sequential progression and independence
UPSC trap: Hydrological drought can persist even after Meteorological drought ends (lag effect)
Agricultural drought's dependence on soil moisture deficit vs. rainfall deficit — not the same trigger
Socioeconomic drought as a policy/governance failure overlay on physical drought

concepts.name: Meteorological Drought: IMD Definition and Rainfall Deficiency Thresholds
key_dimensions: IMD defines: Rainfall deficiency of 26–50% = Moderate Drought; >50% = Severe Drought
UPSC trap: Meteorological drought is region-specific — normal rainfall varies by homogeneous zone
Distinction between 'drought year' and 'drought-affected area' in IMD's classification
Role of El Niño, Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), and weakened monsoon as meteorological triggers

concepts.name: Drought Indices: SPI, PDSI, and NDVI — Measurement and Application
key_dimensions: Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI): multi-scale, probabilistic — used for early warning
Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI): incorporates temperature and soil moisture — better for agricultural drought
NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index): remote sensing tool — used in India's drought assessment via NRSC
UPSC trap: SPI can be calculated for different time scales (1-month, 3-month, 12-month) — each captures different drought type

concepts.name: India's Drought Prone Areas: Geography and Vulnerability Mapping
key_dimensions: Areas receiving <750mm annual rainfall classified as drought-prone — covers ~33% of India's geographical area
Chronic drought zones: Rajasthan, parts of Gujarat, Marathwada, Telangana, Bundelkhand, interior Karnataka
UPSC trap: Not all drought-prone areas are arid — semi-arid regions with erratic rainfall (e.g., Vidarbha) are highly vulnerable
Drought Atlas of India (NRSA/NRSC) and its role in vulnerability zoning

concepts.name: Drought Declaration Mechanism in India: Role of State and Central Governments
key_dimensions: Drought declaration is a State subject — State governments declare drought based on defined criteria
Manual for Drought Management (MoDWR, 2016): four-trigger system — Rainfall, Crop situation, Water levels, Remote sensing indicators
UPSC trap: Central Government does NOT declare drought — it only releases funds; States declare
Inter-ministerial Central Team (IMCT) visits — role in assessing State's memorandum for NDRF release

concepts.name: National Disaster Relief Fund (NDRF) vs. State Disaster Relief Fund (SDRF): Drought Financing
key_dimensions: SDRF is the first line of response — Center contributes 75% (90% for special category states); State 25%
NDRF is supplementary — released only when SDRF is insufficient and IMCT visit validates the claim
UPSC trap: NDRF is not the same as PM Relief Fund or PM CARES — confusion frequently tested
15th Finance Commission changes to SDRF/NDRF allocation norms and drought-specific provisions

concepts.name: Manual for Drought Management 2016: Four-Trigger Framework
key_dimensions: Trigger 1: Rainfall deficiency (>19% below normal in a meteorological sub-division)
Trigger 2: Field indicators — dry spells, crop sowing data, soil moisture anomaly
Trigger 3: Remote sensing indicators — NDVI, Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI)
Trigger 4: Groundwater and reservoir levels — hydrological indicators
UPSC trap: All four triggers need not be simultaneously triggered — State uses composite assessment

concepts.name: Drought and Groundwater Depletion: The Hydrological Feedback Loop
key_dimensions: Over-extraction of groundwater during drought years accelerates long-term hydrological drought
UPSC trap: Groundwater depletion is both a consequence AND a cause of drought intensification
Critical groundwater-stressed blocks (CGWB classification) — overlap with drought-prone districts
Jal Shakti Abhiyan and Atal Bhujal Yojana as policy responses to groundwater-drought nexus

concepts.name: El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and Indian Monsoon Drought Correlation
key_dimensions: El Niño (warming of central/eastern Pacific) statistically linked to below-normal Indian monsoon
UPSC trap: El Niño does NOT always cause drought in India — 1997 El Niño year had above-normal monsoon
Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) as a modulator — positive IOD can offset El Niño's negative effect
La Niña's association with above-normal monsoon — asymmetry with El Niño's effect

concepts.name: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY): Drought Coverage and Limitations
key_dimensions: PMFBY covers prevented sowing, mid-season adversity (including drought), and post-harvest losses
Area-based approach (IUA — Insurance Unit Area) — individual farmer losses may not be compensated if area-average is normal
UPSC trap: PMFBY is not a drought relief measure per se — it is a crop insurance scheme; drought triggers a claim, not automatic relief
Revised PMFBY (2020): States can opt out; premium restructured — impact on drought-prone state coverage

concepts.name: Integrated Drought Management: Mitigation vs. Relief — Policy Distinction
key_dimensions: Mitigation (long-term): watershed development, rainwater harvesting, crop diversification, drought-resistant varieties
Relief (short-term): cash transfers, food distribution, MGNREGS activation, fodder camps
UPSC trap: India's drought policy historically relief-centric — shift towards mitigation is a key policy evolution
National Water Mission (NWM) under NAPCC — drought mitigation as a climate adaptation strategy

concepts.name: MGNREGS as a Drought Response Tool: Design and Limitations
key_dimensions: MGNREGS provides 100 days guaranteed wage employment — activated/expanded during drought as livelihood buffer
Water conservation works under MGNREGS (ponds, check dams) serve dual purpose: relief + long-term mitigation
UPSC trap: MGNREGS is demand-driven — works only if workers register demand; passive households may be excluded
Extension to 150 days allowed in drought-notified areas — a critical exception to the standard 100-day norm

concepts.name: Drought-Resistant Crop Varieties and Agronomic Practices: Technological Interventions
key_dimensions: ICAR's drought-tolerant varieties: Sahbhagi Dhan (rice), DRR Dhan 42, MACS 6222 (wheat) — developed under NICRA
System of Rice Intensification (SRI) — reduces water use by 30–50%; relevant for drought-prone irrigated areas
UPSC trap: Drought-resistant ≠ Drought-proof — these varieties tolerate moisture stress but still require minimum water
National Initiative on Climate Resilient Agriculture (NICRA) — integrates drought adaptation into farming systems

concepts.name: Watershed Development as a Structural Drought Mitigation Strategy
key_dimensions: Watershed approach: treats catchment as unit — integrates soil conservation, water harvesting, and groundwater recharge
Integrated Watershed Management Programme (IWMP) — merged into PMKSY (Watershed Component) in 2015
UPSC trap: Watershed development addresses both drought AND flood — it is a dual-hazard mitigation tool
Per Drop More Crop (PMKSY sub-component) — micro-irrigation linkage to drought management

concepts.name: Drought and Food Security: PDS Activation and Buffer Stock Norms
key_dimensions: Food Corporation of India (FCI) buffer stocks used to stabilize prices and supply during drought-induced shortage
UPSC trap: Minimum buffer stock norms are different from strategic reserves — buffer stocks have quarterly revision
National Food Security Act (NFSA) 2013 — entitlements continue during drought; States must ensure supply
Open Market Sale Scheme (OMSS) — FCI sells grain in open market to control inflation during drought years

concepts.name: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and Drought: India's Commitments
key_dimensions: Sendai Framework (2015–2030): Shift from disaster management to disaster risk reduction (DRR)
Priority 1: Understanding disaster risk — drought risk atlases, vulnerability mapping
India's National DRR Plan (2016) — drought listed under hydro-meteorological hazards with specific targets
UPSC trap: Sendai Framework is NOT a legally binding treaty — it is a voluntary framework; distinction from Paris Agreement

concepts.name: Urban Drought: Emerging Concept and Cape Town 'Day Zero' Analogy
key_dimensions: Urban drought: city-level water scarcity despite possible regional rainfall — driven by infrastructure failure and demand surge
Chennai water crisis (2019) as India's 'Day Zero' moment — groundwater depletion + failed monsoon + poor urban water management
UPSC trap: Urban drought is not officially classified under India's drought management framework — it falls under urban water management
AMRUT 2.0 and Smart Cities Mission — urban water security as indirect drought risk mitigation

concepts.name: Flash Drought: Definition, Detection Challenges, and Climate Change Linkage
key_dimensions: Flash drought: rapid onset (days to weeks) driven by temperature spikes and high evapotranspiration — distinct from slow-onset meteorological drought
Difficult to predict with conventional models — requires high-frequency soil moisture and evaporation data
UPSC trap: Flash drought is primarily driven by heat stress and evapotranspiration, NOT necessarily by rainfall deficiency alone
Climate change increasing flash drought frequency — IPCC AR6 linkage to intensified hydrological cycle

concepts.name: Drought and Internal Migration: Socioeconomic Consequences and Policy Response
key_dimensions: Drought-induced distress migration — movement from Bundelkhand, Marathwada, Telangana to urban centers documented
Economic Survey data and NSSO surveys on climate-linked migration — policy gap in acknowledging 'climate migrants'
UPSC trap: India has no legal category of 'climate/drought refugee' — domestic migrants lack specific legal protection
Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act (1979) — limitations in covering drought-driven seasonal migrants

concepts.name: National Drought Proofing Strategy: Institutional Architecture (NDMA, CWC, IMD, NRSC)
key_dimensions: NDMA: policy framework and guidelines for drought management — not operational agency
IMD: rainfall monitoring, seasonal forecast, drought early warning — Meteorological Drought Watch
CWC: reservoir storage monitoring, river flow data — hydrological drought tracking
NRSC (ISRO): remote sensing-based crop condition monitoring and drought impact assessment
UPSC trap: No single nodal agency for drought — MoAFW is nodal ministry for drought relief, but MoJSW handles water; coordination gap is a frequently tested governance issue
